entries.title: Which code identifies what, who issues it and where to look it up
entries.take: Each code names a different thing. Match the code to what you are describing before you type it into a form.
rows: ISRC
One sound recording or music video
The recording owner, from a prefix an ISRC agency allocates
International ISRC Database; SoundExchange ISRC Search
ISWC
One musical work (the song, not a recording)
A registration agency, usually a society
ISWC-Network, CISAC's public portal
IPI name number
One name a writer or publisher uses
Societies, through the IPI system
Ask your society; the checker here has no look-up
IPI base number
The person or company behind those names
Allocated by the IPI system
Kept private; your society can tell you
ISNI
The public identity of a person, group or company
An ISNI registration agency; isni.org says ISNI is not free
The ISNI database at isni.org
IPN
A performer on recordings, per the MLC
A performers' rights body such as SoundExchange
Ask the performers' rights body

entries.title: Mistake: putting an ISWC in an ISRC field, or the reverse
entries.take: An ISRC names one recording and an ISWC names the song. Each code answers a different question, so the wrong one breaks the link.
entries.body: IFPI says the ISRC is not used for compositions or lyrics. CISAC says the ISWC does not identify recordings or sheet music. A song has one ISWC, but it can have many recordings, such as a studio take and a remix, each with its own ISRC. A mix-up leaves a recording unattached to its song, or the reverse.
do: Copy each code from the register that issued it.
Test a code at /music/tools#identifiers before you submit it.

entries.title: An ISRC is 12 characters: a prefix, a year and a five-digit number
entries.take: Two letters and three letters or digits make the prefix, two digits give the year, and five digits finish it. IFPI describes no check digit.
entries.body: The prefix belongs to the registrant and is allocated by an ISRC agency. The year element takes the final two digits of the assignment year. The five-digit designation code is picked by the registrant from its range and must not repeat within a year. On paper the code takes the letters ISRC in front and hyphens at three points, which are not part of the code. IFPI's validity test is only whether the string fits this layout.
do: Store the 12 characters with no spaces or hyphens.
Check the format at /music/tools#identifiers.

entries.title: Mistake: reading the ISRC's year as the year the track was recorded
entries.take: The two digits show when the code was assigned. IFPI says the recording year belongs in the metadata, not in the code.
entries.body: IFPI says the year of reference is normally, but not always, the year the final master was prepared, and it can differ from the year of recording. It exists so that codes from earlier years cannot be assigned twice. A recording released without an ISRC can be given one later, and the year is then the year of assignment.
do: Keep the recording year in its own field.
Never edit an ISRC to match a date.

entries.title: The recording owner assigns the ISRC, directly or through a manager
entries.take: Normally it is the original owner who assigns a recording's ISRC. Membership of a trade body is not needed, and a distributor can assign on the owner's behalf.
entries.body: IFPI says independent artists, labels and groups can all assign ISRCs, that only the owner may assign to a recording, and that an appointed ISRC manager can do it on the owner's instruction. Most distributors can supply ISRCs or deliver the owner's own. Prefixes come from the agency for your territory; in the US that is the US ISRC Agency at usisrc.org.
do: Ask your distributor which ISRCs it assigned, and keep a copy.

entries.title: US Rights Owner Prefix fee at the US ISRC Agency
entries.unit: one-time fee for a US rights owner prefix
entries.take: The US ISRC Agency charges this once to allocate a prefix to a rights owner and says no further costs follow. Elsewhere, ask your territory's agency.

entries.title: When a recording needs a new ISRC and when it keeps its code
entries.take: A creative change to the recording needs a new ISRC; a new format, release or owner does not. Rows follow IFPI's 2021 Handbook, which qualifies the FAQ's 10-second rule.

entries.title: Check whether a recording already has an ISRC before you assign one
entries.take: IFPI's International ISRC Database and SoundExchange's ISRC Search are both free to search. Neither is guaranteed to list every code.
entries.body: IFPI says its database is powered by repertoire data that rights owners submit to SoundExchange, is updated daily, and matches more loosely than its paid assignment service. A track can be missing because its owner never submitted data or a distributor did not enter it. Codes from IFPI's own online assignment appear after around 10 days.
do: Search by artist and title, not only by code.
Ask a former distributor or label for your ISRCs before you move.

entries.title: Seven facts to keep on file for every ISRC
entries.take: IFPI says anyone assigning ISRCs must keep the code, main artist, title, version title, duration, content type and first publication date.
entries.body: The registrant must give this reference data to IFPI or its designee on request. Content type tells a sound recording from a music video. The first publication date, known as the P-date, ties the code to a specific recording. The version title carries details such as live or extended mix, which is where a remix is told apart from the original.
do: Keep these seven fields for every track in one sheet.

entries.title: An ISWC is T, nine digits and a check digit, under ISO 15707:2022
entries.take: The code names a song as a creation, not a recording. It shows no shares and does not confer copyright.
entries.body: CISAC says the ISWC is a letter T, nine digits for the work and a numeric check digit, written after the letters ISWC, with hyphens or dots allowed for readability. The standard is ISO 15707:2022. The code is permanent: it does not change when a writer moves society or the work enters the public domain. The checker here tests the digit against a published formula, so a pass means consistent, not that the code exists.
do: Test an ISWC at /music/tools#identifiers before you reuse it.

entries.title: Only a registration agency can allocate an ISWC, not the writer or publisher
entries.take: ISWCs come from the society or agency a work is registered with. For new works, registering the work is the step that gets the number.
entries.body: CISAC says creators and publishers may not allocate their own ISWCs, and that a number is assigned as part of registration once all creators are uniquely identified. A publisher can ask its society for access to CISAC's ISWC Allocation Service to get codes before registering. Since a 2020 modernisation ISWCs are assigned centrally, and CISAC says codes can be ready within hours. A society's own numbering system is not replaced, so you will see both.
do: Register the work with your society, then read the ISWC from its catalogue.

entries.title: Mistake: registering a work with a writer who has no IPI, then waiting for an ISWC
entries.take: An ISWC needs every creator identified. A co-writer outside any society can leave the work without a code at first.
entries.body: CISAC says registration needs complete metadata, including the IPI name number and role of every creator, and that a code is allocated only when all creators have been uniquely identified. GEMA gives the same reason when a work lacks an ISWC: a contributor who is not in a society, so not in the IPI database, means no ISWC initially.
do: Collect each co-writer's society and IPI number at the writing session.

entries.title: A work can end up with two ISWCs, and the preferred one is the one to use
entries.take: CISAC says complex registrations have occasionally produced more than one ISWC for a work, and its data marks the preferred one.
entries.body: CISAC's open data lists each Preferred ISWC and any archived code merged into it, and asks users to use the preferred one. Since the 2020 changes, duplicates can be merged, or separated again if joined in error. If two codes appear for one song in your files, ask the society which is preferred rather than choosing one.
do: Refresh stored ISWCs against the society's catalogue each year.

entries.title: IPI numbers identify writers and publishers across the societies' systems
entries.take: The IPI system gives each interested party a base number and each name they use a name number. Societies issue them to members.
entries.body: CISAC says the IPI system identifies a person or company with an interest in a work across roles such as composer, arranger and publisher, and that SUISA administers it under CISAC and BIEM rules. The MLC says the base number is kept private and a name number stands for a public name, such as a stage name. SOCAN says it assigns IPIs to its members and that CAE number is the older term.

entries.title: Mistake: giving a base number where a form asks for an IPI name number
entries.take: People often say IPI for either number. Check which one a form wants, because the base number is the private one.
entries.body: The MLC notes that people usually mean the base number when they say IPI, yet the public number is the name number. GEMA asks for each co-creator's IP name number when you register a work, and says you can look one up in a creator search. The split-sheet generator on this site asks for the name number and flags a base number.
do: Ask your society for the name number of each name you write under.

entries.title: ISNI names a public identity, and anyone can apply through an agency
entries.take: An ISNI identifies a public identity, such as an artist name or a band. CISAC calls it voluntary, and isni.org says it is not free.
entries.body: isni.org says an ISNI identifies public identities of people, organisations and groups, has 16 characters ending in a check character that can be X, and is issued only through registration agencies, which charge fees. CISAC says pseudonyms get separate ISNIs, linked in the database, and that ISNI can act as a bridge to codes like the IPI. The checker here tests the check character.

entries.title: CWR is the bulk file format publishers use to register works with societies
entries.take: Common Works Registration (CWR), a CISAC file format, carries many work registrations at once. The MLC aims it at hundreds or thousands of works.
entries.body: CISAC oversees CWR, and a sender has to be set up with CISAC before using it. Publishers and administrators send registrations in it and get status back from the society. The MLC says it may not suit you without thousands of works; a writer with a few songs uses a portal. Its user guide, dated May 2024 and still the one its help page linked on 20 November 2026, takes versions 2.1 and 2.2 and lists 3.1 as pending. SOCAN says a sub-publisher abroad registers your songs there, by CWR or other means. CISAC's layouts and code lists are not reproduced here.
do: Ask your society or administrator which CWR version it takes.

entries.title: Mistake: sending a CWR registration that omits owners or does not reach 100 percent
entries.take: The MLC wants every party on a work listed, ownership that totals 100 percent, and no unknown flag on a party you control.
entries.body: The MLC's CWR guide (May 2024) asks for ownership records for every party, controlled or not. For each right, ownership shares must total 100 percent, give or take 0.06 points, or zero, and collection shares may not pass 100 percent. Unknown writer or publisher markers are accepted for parties you do not control. A controlled party marked unknown is rejected, because those records form your claim, and a file whose name was used before is rejected too.
do: Check totals and party flags before you send a file.

entries.title: DDEX standards in plain words: what each message carries
entries.take: DDEX has ten families of standards, and anyone may use them with a free licence. Six of them are below, as DDEX describes them.

entries.title: ERN delivers the release; DSR reports what it earned
entries.take: ERN goes from a label or distributor to the store with the release and its terms. DSR comes back from the store with sales and usage.
entries.body: DDEX says ERN tells a digital service about releases and resources, such as recordings and videos, and the terms on which they can be offered. DSR is the report the service sends back so the rights owner can invoice for rights used. As of 20 November 2026 DDEX names ERN 4.3.2 as the latest published version and urges 4.3.x. DSR is a flat-file standard with profiles for different business models. The AI page covers the ERN flags for generative AI.
do: Ask your distributor which ERN version it sends.

entries.title: DDEX messages are checked against a schema, and invalid ones should be rejected
entries.take: DDEX offers a free online validator. Recipients should reject invalid messages, and senders should validate before sending.
entries.body: DDEX lists grounds for rejection: failing the XML schema, breaking the profile rules, breaking extra rules the two sides agreed, plain inconsistencies such as different display artists at release and track level for a single, and blank tags in fields that must be filled. Recipients should not guess missing data. DDEX says its validator does not store uploaded messages.
do: Run a validation before every delivery.

entries.title: Which US copyright application fits a song, a recording or both
entries.take: The Copyright Office treats the song and the recording as two works. One application can cover both only if both are on the same phonorecord and one party claims both.
rows: An artist records someone else's song
Apply for the recording only
A songwriter whose song others record
Apply for the song only
A songwriter records their own song
One application for both is possible
A record company owns the song and the recording
It may use one application for both
The same owner also sells sheet music and the album
Two applications, each with its own deposit
The Single Application
Same phonorecord, one performer-author, and sole owner of both

entries.title: What a US copyright registration adds, as Circular 1 states it
entries.take: Registration adds a public record, a route to court for US works and, if made in time, stronger remedies. Protection itself does not depend on it.
entries.body: Circular 1 lists the advantages: a public record of the authorship and ownership facts; registration, or refusal, before a suit over a US work; prima facie evidence of validity when it comes before publication or within the first five years after it; and eligibility for statutory damages and attorneys' fees when it precedes infringement or comes within three months of publication. Circular 56 says registration is not required for protection. When to register, or sue, is a question for a copyright lawyer.

entries.title: Register a song with the Copyright Office: the application points to get right
entries.take: Choose Work of the Performing Arts, give the title as written, state who wrote what, and name any pre-existing material.
entries.body: Circular 50 says to give the title exactly as it is printed on the work, say whether it is published, and give the year of completion. The author is whoever wrote the music and lyrics, or the employer where the song was made for hire. Describe authorship as lyrics, music or arrangement, and list pre-existing material in the limitation of claim. An application needs a form, a nonrefundable fee and a deposit copy.
do: Check current fees on copyright.gov before you file.

entries.title: Register a recording: choose Sound Recording and send the right deposit
entries.take: Choose Sound Recording and name its authors. Upload the file if it is unpublished or digital-only; send the CD or LP if it came out on one.
entries.body: Circular 56 says an unpublished or digital-only recording should be uploaded as a digital file, up to 500 MB each, with no physical copy as well. A recording published on CD or LP is deposited in that physical format. One published in the US may need a pair of best-edition copies, with CD ranked first. A derivative recording, such as a mashup, must name its pre-existing material in the limitation of claim. The basics page covers who counts as an author.
do: Confirm who the authors are before you file.

entries.title: Group options let one fee cover several songs, several recordings or an album
entries.take: Up to ten unpublished songs, or ten unpublished recordings, can go on one application if the same authors are all named as claimants.
entries.body: Circulars 50 and 56 describe group registration of unpublished works by the same authors. For songs, the Office says naming a performing group alone is not enough: every individual who contributed authorship must be named. Circular 56 also covers registering an album as a collective work, and a unit of publication for recordings packaged with artwork. Circular 34 has the rules.

entries.title: Each co-writer has to be registered with their own society too
entries.take: Registering a song with one society does not register your co-writers elsewhere. Each registers it with their own society.
entries.body: GEMA says each creator must register a work with their own society, so a SACEM member registers with SACEM, and asks you to enter co-creators' IP name numbers and pass on the ISWC. SOCAN says that if your co-writer is not a member, you can register the song with the shares and be paid your portion, but that co-writer is not paid until joining SOCAN or a society it works with abroad.
do: Share the ISWC and splits with every co-writer.

entries.title: GEMA: shares add to 100 percent per role, and late registrations are not paid
entries.take: GEMA's portal wants shares per role that total 100, and a work registered after the deadline is left out of the distribution.
entries.body: GEMA says performing and mechanical shares, if entered, must add to 100 percent per role, and are mandatory only in the publisher section. Blank creator shares are split evenly by role. For works used in a calendar year, the cut-off falls on 31 January in the year after use, with other deadlines for some categories. A late work is not counted and gives no right to claim, which GEMA ties to its distribution plan. GEMA says the ISWC follows once the work reaches registration status 1.
do: Register new works as soon as the split is agreed.

entries.title: A society's own work number is not the ISWC
entries.take: SOCAN gives its own Work Number, and a temporary code is replaced by the international ISWC a few weeks after registration.
entries.body: SOCAN says a new work first gets a temporary code, replaced by the ISWC a few weeks later and visible in the member portal catalogue. The Work Number is SOCAN-specific and appears on statements and in its public repertoire search. In Canada, SOCAN says, an ISRC for a recording can be requested from SOPROQ.
do: Give the ISWC, not a society's work number, to people outside that society.

entries.title: Before release: a metadata checklist for the song and the recording
entries.take: Tick what applies. The registers differ, so check each one separately, and use the same names and splits in all of them.

entries.title: Mistake: entering a writer or publisher name that does not match the IPI record
entries.take: Registers match people on name and number. Use the spelling your society holds, with the IPI number where a form asks for it.
entries.body: The MLC's CWR guide says a publisher sending files must give its name as the IPI database lists it for its IPI name number. In the MLC portal you can search writers by name or IPI number, and it shows existing writers that match what you enter, so you avoid duplicates. GEMA says to look a co-creator up in a creator search, and to enter the creator manually if identical names leave you unsure. The MLC says accurate matching data is what gets you paid correctly and on time.
do: Copy names from your society's record, not from memory.

entries.title: Style guide: credit featured artists in the artist field, spelled the same everywhere
entries.take: The Music Biz style guide, version 2.1, advises putting featured artists in the artist role rather than the title, with one spelling per name.
entries.body: Music Biz's Music Metadata Style Guide, version 2.1 of September 2015, advises crediting featured artists at the artist role level unless a contract says otherwise, using only 'feat.' and 'with' where a title shows them, one spelling of each artist and label name across deliveries, and a copyright line of first publication year and holder. It is voluntary guidance, and each store applies its own rules.
do: Ask your distributor how it wants featured artists entered.

circ-56.support: Sound recording defined; distinct from song and phonorecord; authors are featured performer and producer unless work made for hire; recordings after 1 January 1978 protected on fixation; registration not required; digital performance right only.

gema-deadline.support: Works used in a calendar year: deadline 31 January of the next year; other deadlines by category; late works not counted give no right to claim (section 36 of the distribution plan).
